His case in short was that the suit property, a homestead land measuring 153 acres, including houses, structures, attached garden and appurtenances with all casement right thereof in Chittagong town belonged to the defendant No. 1, a Christian widow, her minor daughter defendant No. 2 and her stepson defendant No. 3 in equal 1/3rd shares. On 10-12-59, the defendant No. 1, on her own behalf and on behalf of her minor daughter, and-defendant No. 3 entered into a contract, vide Exhibit 1, for selling the suit property to the plaintiff for Rs. 6,000. The defendants 1 and 3 jointly received Rs. 2,000 as earnest money on that day and promised to execute the Kabala by 17-1-1961 after receiving the balances consideration money. They however subsequently changed their minds and did not execute the Kabala On 8-1-1961 the plaintiff served a legal notice on them offering the balance consideration money on receipt of which the defendant No. 3 alone executed a Kabala for his1/3rd share in the suij property on 27-1-1961 after receiving Rs. 1,480. This Kabala was registered after an appeal under the Registration Act. Plaintiff then transferred some portion of his purchased land to one Tofail Ahmed by a registered Kabala dated 4-5-62. Before his transfer to the plaintiff on 27-1-61, the defendant No. 3 had already transferred, some of the land in suit to defendants 4 & 5 who purchased the same knowingly of the plaintiff's contract with defendants 1-3. Plaintiff filed his suit not only against defendants 1-3, but also against defendants 4-5. 

 6. BB Roy Chowdhury refers to two decisions, wherein, he claims, the powers of a Christian mother have received judicial elucidation. The first case is that of Bangrammal vs Lydia Kant reported in AIR 1934 Mad 605. Referring to an earlier decision of the Madras High Court, reported in AIR 1931 Mad 529, it was held therein that amongst the (Indian) Christian community an act done by a mere de facto guardian (such as a sister's husband) will not bind the minor and will be void against him. "But a mother", goes the decision "the father being dead, does not, we think, fall within this category, but is certainly, for many purposes, the natural guardian of her minor child. She is, for instance, entitled to the custody of the child and to the guardianship of its property." A Christian mother in the decision under reference alienated her two minor daughters shares by executing a sale-deed. One of the daughters on attaining majority, sued for a declaration that the sale was not binding upon her and for partition and delivery of her one-third share in the property. The Madras High Court held that an alienation by a Christian mother as natural guardian would be voidable, not void. 

 7. The next case cited by Mr Roy Chowdhury is that of Decosta vs Naddar, reported in AIR 1956 (Trav-Coch) 107. In this case too a Christian minor on attaining majority claimed that his mother was not competent to alienate the properties so as to defeat the title of the plaintiff. This decision followed AIR 1934 Mad 605. It held that the sale-deed affected by the mother is binding on the plaintiff unless he avoids it within 3 years of attaining majority. The following passage from Trevelyan's aforequoted book, in its 6th edition at PP. 167-168 (P. 60 of the 5th edition) was quoted in the decision:— 

 9. The present case, however, is not a case of completed alienation by a Christian mother of her ward's property. It is a case of specific performance of contract where alienation is sought to be completed with the aid of the Court. It is, therefore, not relevant far the purpose of this case to consider whether an alienation by a Christian mother of her ward's property is void or voidable. That question may properly be raised in a case where alienation is completed and is a past transaction and all that remains for the minor, is either to accept or avoid it on attaining majority. The two decisions cited are not, therefore, exactly on the point. The questioning this case is, where the natural guardian of a Christian minor's estate makes an executory contract for the sale of immovable property, can the contract be specifically enforced against the minor? 

 10. The general principle is well established now that an executory contract for the purchase of sale of immovable property cannot be specifically enforced either by or on behalf of the minor or against the minor or against his property. A partial exception to this general principle is made with regard to contracts entered into on behalf of minors by guardians who have the power under the law to bind the minors by their, acts. This partial exception to the general principle has been well formulated in the case of guardians under Muslim law and Hindu law. But the forensic law of this sub-continent is scarce indeed in its treatment of this partial exception in the case of guardians amongst communities other than Muslims and Hindus. 

 11. Mr BK Das submits, and it appears to me to be correct, however, that in granting or refusing specific performance of contract of sale of a Christian minor's property, the Court will be guided by the same considerations which govern the same relief is respect of a Muslim minor's property or a Hindu minor's property. The Court will require of the plaintiff to satisfy itself whether the contract was for the benefit of the minor, whether there was any legal necessity involved therein, whether it will be possible for the minor to avoid the contract on attaining majority. Section 27 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 imposes obligations upon all guardians of the property of award to deal there with as carefully as a wan of ordinary prudence would deal with it. Such a view will not be inconsistent with that Act. Even in Bangrammal's case, (AIR 1934 Mad 605) cited by Mr Roy Chowdhury and in the case reported in AIR 1931 Mad 529, it was inquired into whether the sale-deed was executed in the interest of the minor, Trevelyan also says at P. 167 of his aforequoted book (5th edition); 

 12. It is clear that even though a Christian mother as a natural guardian of her minor children can enter into an executory contract of sale in respect of her minor children's property, in decreeing specific performance thereof the Court will have to be satisfied inter alia that the contract has endured to the minor's benefit No such case has been made out. It is neither averred in the plaint nor given in evidence that the contract is for the benefit of defendant No. 2. There is total absence of any evidence in this regard, which it was for the plaintiff to adduce. In view of the matter I am of the opinion that i that the two Courts below did not commit any illegality in refusing specific performance against defendant No. 2, although their reasoning there of proceeded along different lines. 

 "Received with thanks a sum of Rs. 2,000 (rupees two thousand only) by way of earnest money from Mr Archana Prasad Nandy S/o Birendrz Lai Nandy of Village Kanchana, PS Satkania, Chittagong." at present residing at 21, Alkaran Lane, PS Kotwali, Chittagong, out of the total consideration of Rs 6,000 (Rupees six thousand only) for which we agree to sell our properties shown in schedule below. We shall execute and get the kabala registered within 17th day of January, 1961, on receipt of residue of Rs. 4,000 (rupees four thousand only) from the said Mr Archana Prasad Nandy. In case of our failure to complete the sale by the aforesaid, date the said Mr Archana Prasad Nandy shall be at liberty to get the kabala executed and registered through Court I. Margaret Randolph, for myself and my daughter Chilia Randolph and IAP Randolph sign this document." 

 This document than contains case contract schedule of land agreed to be sold, recital of payment of Rs. 2,000 followed by the signatures of 4 witnesses and the signatures of defendants 1 & 3 in the margin. 

 15. The question is, can a part of the above contract be given effect to in terms of Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act? The general rule of equity is that the Court will not compel specific performance of a contract unless it can enforce the whole contract. This rule is embodied in section 17 of the Specific Relief Act. Under Section 17 a contract cannot be specifically enforced in part except under situations provided for under sections 14, 15 & 16 of the said Act, sections 14 & 16 of the said Act, con-cedes Mr Roy Chowdhury, have no application to this case. He submits that section 15 has full application to this case. Before I consider the application of section 15, let me set it out in full:— 

 As one can see, there are several conditions for the application of section 15, Without going into those conditions the words in the beginning of the section "where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it" may be noticed. Sarkar says in his commentary on the Specific Relief Act (9th edition 1958) at P. 91, "These words suggest that section 15 is applicable only where the defendant made a representation that the whole of the property belonged to her, which eventually turns out not to be correct. The section has no application where the defendant contracted on his or her behalf and on behalf of somebody else (say, a minor) and it is found that the contract is not enforceable in law so far as that somebody is concerned". Sarkar has further observed in the next breath, "The Calcutta High Court has, however, applied section 15 in such cases also". 

 16. The earliest case on record is that of Abdul Hug vs Mohammad Yehia Khan, reported in AIR 1924 Pat. 81. An agreement for sale of certain immovable properties was executed by defendant No. 1 and by defendant No. 2 for self and as guardian of defendants 3 and 4. It was held that defendant No. 2 as de facto guardian had no power to convey to the plaintiff the shares of defendants 3 and 4. It was thereafter held as follows:— 

 The decision goes further to state that for want of mutuality in the contract the plaintiff's present willingness to take a conveyance of the shares of defendants 1 & 2 cannot be conceded. That was not the original bargain struck between the parties. The decision quoted the following dictum of Lindley LJ in the case of Lumley vs Ravenscroft (1895) 1 QB 683 (H), "This case is not within the exception as to misconduct... but comes within the general rule that where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another specific performance will not be granted against him as to his shares." In interpreting Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, the above observations of Lindley LJ obviously carried some weight. It was held on a consideration of sections 14-16, that it was impossible to give the plaintiff a decree for specific performance as against defendants 1 and 2. 

 17. Mr BK Das has cited the case of Rameswar vs Anandin, reported in AIR 1956 (Pat) 53. That was a case where the defendant contracted on her own behalf and on behalf of her minor daughter and it was found that the contract was not enforceable against the daughter. Following the earlier Patna case it has been held therein, "Defendant 1 did not make any representation that the whole of the property, the subject matter of the contract, belonged to her. She had made a contract on her behalf and on behalf of somebody else, and it has been found that the contract is not enforceable in law so far as that somebody is concerned. To such a case, section 15 has no application." The decision quotes the reasoning of the earlier Patna case and also quotes Fry on Specific Performance, Chapter XVI, Article 823, as follows, in support of its opinion:— 

 "823. A contract for the sale of property in one lot will generally be considered indivisible. Thus, in a case where. two undivided seventh shares of land were sold in one lot, the Court refused to enforce specific performance where a good title could be made to one seventh only and the purchaser of the entirety will, of course, not be compelled to take six undivided seventh parts of the estate. And so in a case where two persons were owners of an estate in undivided moieties and the plaintiff's sought to enforces an alleged contract by them to lease the coals under it, but could not prove any such contract against one of the owners, one ground on which the bill was dismissed against the other owner also was that he had never contracted to lease one share alone. 

 If he had held himself out and contracted as the owner of the whole, the case would have been different. But in the absence of misrepresentation or misconduct, the genera rule is that where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another person, and purports to deal with the entirety, specific performance will not be granted against him as to share." 

 As already said, the Calcutta High Court has applied section 15 in such cases also. Mr BB Roy Chowdhury has cited the case of Puma vs Gopendra, reported in AIR 1976 Cal 744. That was a case where A entered into a contract for safe of his share of property together with the share of his minor nephew B. On the view that A "was perfectly entitled to enter into an agreement with respect to his own share of the property, without reference to the interest of his infant nephew, it held that there is nothing in law to prevent the plaintiffs from enforcing the con tract as against A with regard to share of the property. Section 15 was therefore held to be applicable to the contract. This case neither gives any reason for the decision nor explains how the language of section 15 is applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 18. Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited next the case of Dihedral vs Monomohon, AIR 1957 Cal. 209 which is a case of lease. A contract of lease entered into by defendants 1-4 was found to be not binding on minor defendant No. 2. Specific performance was granted in respect of 3/4th share of adult contesting defendants but in this case also no independent reason has been furnished. 

 19. Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited another decision, the case of Imam Din vs Muhammad Din reported in AIR 1926 Lah 137. The High Court granted specific performance of contract against defendant No. 1 in respect of his own share in the suit property when it was found that he had no right to sell the share of defendant No. 2, his minor nephew. Section 15 has been made applicable to the case. No reason has been advanced for this decision also. 

 Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited next a decision of the Privy Council, the case of Abdul Karim vs Gladys Muriel, reported in 54 CWN 770. This was an appeal from West Africa decided in 1948 In this Decision the Privy Council says that Lindley, LJ's dictum in Lumley vs Ravenscroft (prey cited) that "where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another person and purports to deal with the entirety, specific performance will no be granted against him as to his share" "is seriously diminished by the circumstances to which they have adverted'. Lumley's case, the Privy Council seems to think, is no answer to the position where there is more than one vendor and one of the vendors cannot complete the contract. In this case the appellant had agreed to buy two houses which were owned by the 1st 2nd and 3rd respondents as tenants in common contract was unenforceable against the 1st respondent as she had no power to make the contract. The Privy Council held, on the authority of Horrocks vs Rigby (1878) 9 Ch D 180 and Attorney-General vs Day 1 Yes Sen 218 that the appellant can enforce it against the22nd and 3rd respondents in respect of their /1rd shares. Mr, Roy Chowdhury heavily relies upon this decision and submits that the present case is a case of more than one vendor. 

 20. It is no doubt apparent that to the extent that the decision reported in AIR 1924 (Pat) 81 and AIR 1956 (Pat) 53 are based on the afore-quoted dictum of Lindley of LJ., their validity can now be doubted on the authority of the just cited Privy Council case. But the Patna decisions did not rest on the dictum of Liodley, LJ alone. Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act has been connected with the dictum of Lindley, LJ Specific Relief Act has not been considered by the Privy Council whose decision is based entirely on a consideration of the English law on the subject. And I get it from the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Specific Relief Bill, "It seems impossible to elicit a Consistent doctrine from the English decisions as to the right of a purchaser or lessee to specific performance with abatement or compensation when the title of the persons agreeing to sell or lease is defective (Quoted in Sarkar's Specific Relief Act, 9th Edition pp. 89-90). That is why section 15 was introduced and it was a clear departure from the English rule as to abatement or compensation when specific performance of a part of a contract is decreed. It is difficult, therefore, to accept the Privy Council decision, cited by Mr Chowdhury, as an authority in support of his submission. As observed by the Privy Council itself in the case William Graham vs Krishna Chandra Dey, in AIR 1925 (PC) 45, Section 14 to 17 inclusive of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, are both positive and negative in their forms. Taken together, they constitute a complete code, within the terms of which specific performance of con tracts must be brought, if it is to be granted at all. Although assistance may be derived from a consideration of cases upon this branch of English jurisprudence, the language of the sections must ultimately prevail". 

 22. The fourth submission of Mr BB Roy Chowdhury must be held to be correct. Time was not of the essence of the contract in this case and the very despatch of legal notice dated 8-6-61 offering to pay the balance consideration money was a good offer. In that view of the matter, the finding of the appellate court below that the plaintiff did not perform his part of the contract is not sustainable. 

 26. But that the defendants 1 & 3 executed the contract dated 10-12-59, and received Rs. 2,000 from the plaintiff as earnest money stand as a concurrently concluded fact. The plaintiff, therefore, cannot be denied any relief in this case. He should not be driven to a separate suit for realisation of the earnest money, of Rs. 2,000 from defendants 1 & 3. I therefore, pass a decree in favour of the plaintiff directing defendants 1 & 3 to return, to the plaintiff the earnest money of Tk. 2,000 with interest thereon at 11% per annum from 17-1-61 to the date of payment. Defendants 1&2 shall pay the plaintiff, costs in both the Courts below. There will be no order as to costs in this appeal. The appeal is disposed of in the above terms.
